title: Hemiconvulsion-Hemiplegia-Epilepsy syndrome in a 3-year-old girl: A case report and literature review
case_prompt:
A 3-year-old girl, second child of healthy nonconsanguineous parents, had normal prenatal history and developmental milestones until age 2. At that time, she had prolonged focal seizures involving the left side of her body that required multiple antiepileptic drugs for control. After discharge, she remained on sodium valproate and was seizure-free but developed persistent weakness of the left upper and lower limbs. She was referred for evaluation of ongoing hemiparesis and delayed psychomotor development. 

On examination, her growth parameters were appropriate for age. Neurologic examination revealed spastic left hemiparesis and delayed motor milestones; other systems were unremarkable. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed marked atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere with ex-vacuot dilatation of the ipsilateral ventricle and hyperintense signal in the subcortical white matter on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke — “abnormalities that are not confined to a specific vascular territory and by normal findings on angio-MRI.”  
2. Dyke-Davidoff-Masson syndrome — “characterized by cerebral hemi-atrophy along with ipsilateral calvarial thickening and hyper-pneumatization of paranasal air sinuses.”  
3. Sturge–Weber syndrome — “cerebral hemi-atrophy typically localized to the parieto-occipital area, often accompanied by ipsilateral enlargement of the choroid plexus and prominent leptomeningeal enhancement.”  
4. Rasmussen encephalitis — “initial atrophy is typically observed in the ipsilateral caudate nucleus, followed by more generalized hemisphere atrophy and signal changes.”
